content: Residual neuromuscular blockade is linked to significant postoperative complications. Some anesthesiologists administer neostigmine to reverse neuromuscular blockade in all pediatric surgical patients. However, the incidence of residual neuromuscular blockade may be lower in pediatric patients compared to adults. The administration of neostigmine has been associated with adverse effects, including postoperative nausea, vomiting, excessive salivation, and bradycardia. This raises an important question for pediatric anesthesiologists: should neostigmine be routinely used to reverse neuromuscular blockade in every pediatric patient? The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the routine use of neostigmine is necessary to prevent residual neuromuscular blockade in pediatric patients who have received muscle relaxants. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, up to August 2013. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing neostigmine with placebo in pediatric surgical patients classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II. The participants were required to be younger than 12 years of age, including newborns, and to have received non-depolarizing muscle relaxants. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. One study was found but is awaiting classification. Consequently, no RCTs were available to either support or refute the routine use of neostigmine for reversing neuromuscular blockade in pediatric patients.
